title: Graceful decommission, hotpatching, and fallback procedure (draft)
body:
Purpose:
This is a working draft runbook for: graceful node decommissioning (planned maintenance), emergency hotpatching of GPU drivers or kernel modules on live nodes, and automated fallback paths when a node or GPU exhibits degraded behavior. Goal is to reduce blast radius during infra upgrades and speed recovery for oncall.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to k8s GPU-backed node pools used by Redwood serving-runtime (prod and staging).
- Assumes standard SRE tooling available: kubectl, gcloud/az/eksctl, cluster-autoscaler hooks, node-exporter metrics, Prometheus alerts, and our capacity-injector tool.
- Not covering hardware-level physical GPU swaps (separate HW swap playbook exists). This focuses on software-driven replacement, cordon/drain, live hotpatch, and rapid capacity add.

Quick decision checklist (oncall):
- Is traffic routed through a load-balancer or gateway that supports gradual route removal? (yes -> proceed with canary drain; no -> full drain)
- Is the node under active long-running KV cache sessions? (if yes, delay drain or use cache-proxy fallback)
- Are there < 2 spare nodes available in the AZ? (if yes, consider immediate capacity injection)
- Does the GPU driver/kernel change require reboot? (if yes, schedule maintenance window unless emergency)

Pre-maintenance prep (planned):
- Validate image/driver hotpatch in a staging GPU pool. Attach test workload for 30–60m.
- Create a temp rollback image tag and stash in artifact repo.
- Notify: #sre, #serving-runtime, oncall pager and product-impact channel at T-60m.
- Confirm autoscaler policy: min nodes reduced to allow scale-out for replacement capacity.
- Add maintenance marker in the console (redwood-console: maintenance -> add note).

Emergency triage (symptoms: GPU ECC errors, kernel oopses, driver hang, NodeReady flapping):
1) Immediately set node to unschedulable: kubectl cordon <node> # prevents new pods.
2) Capture state: kubectl describe node; journalctl -k /var/log/kern.log; nvidia-smi -q (if available); dmesg | tail -n 200. Upload logs to incident ticket.
3) If pods are actively failing, check pod restart counts and pod logs for model-serving containers.
4) If behavior indicates kernel panic or host-level hang: attempt ssh and run a lightweight diagnostic script (/usr/local/bin/sre-node-diagnostic) to snapshot memory, processes, and NVidia driver state.
5) If ssh fails or node is unresponsive: mark as NotReady in cluster UI and escalate to infra-hardware oncall.

Cordon and drain guidelines (graceful):
- prefer kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --timeout=30m --grace-period=60 <node>
- When draining model-serving pods, prefer rollout to a compatible model variant on other nodes (use the rollout script that swaps traffic to v2 variants).
- For pods that depend on local cache volume: follow cache migration steps: pause writes, snapshot, start a warmup copy on target node, then resume writes once warm.
- If drain stalls due to PV detach or CSI timeouts: escalate to storage-sre and consider --force after 15m if it's safe. Document reasons in ticket.

Hotpatch path (software driver/kernel upgrade without full reboot):
- Only allowed if validated in staging and kernel livepatching supported by distro (Ubuntu livepatch or kpatch).
- Steps: ensure node has no critical production-only pods (cordon + drain noncritical).
- Run livepatch agent: sudo canonical-livepatch enable <token> OR sudo kpatch load <module>.
- Verify driver stack: nvidia-smi; ldconfig; restart container runtime if needed (systemctl restart containerd) — prefer restarting only runtime, not entire host.
- Run smoke tests: send small inference requests to the node's health-check endpoint and verify latency and stability for 10m.
- If issues appear within 15m, rollback livepatch (kpatch unload) and restart runtime with previous driver. If rollback fails, schedule node reboot into previous image.

Automated fallback (rapid capacity add):
- If loss of >10% GPU capacity in an AZ or pool and average latency > SLO, trigger capacity-injector script to add equivalent vGPU capacity in the same region (adds nodes with pre-baked image).
- Monitor for autoscaler thrash; set temporary 5m cooldown.
- If capacity add fails due to cloud quota, open an urgent cloud-quota ticket and shift traffic to alternate region via traffic-router policy.

Post-incident tasks (oncall -> SRE owner):
- Record timeline in incident ticket (include cordon/drain timestamps, hotpatch start/rollback if any, capacity-add events).
- Collect metrics: per-route latency, pod restarts, GPU utilization, node reboot counts.
- Add follow-up items: improved alerting thresholds, runbook clarifications, and automation gaps.

Communications templates (short):
- Slack incident start (channel): "INVESTIGATING: Node <node> in <pool> showing GPU driver instability. Cordoning + draining. Impact: degraded capacity for model X. Oncall: @pager."
- Customer-facing (minimal): "We are investigating elevated latency for some requests. We have activated mitigation to reduce impact and will update in 30 minutes."

Operator command cheat-sheet (quick copy):
- kubectl cordon <node>
- kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --timeout=30m --grace-period=60\- kubectl describe node <node>
- kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>
- gcloud compute instances reset <instance> --zone=<z> (or aws ec2 reboot-instances)\- nvidia-smi -q\- journalctl -u containerd -n 200

Open questions / TODOs (draft):
- Should we allow hotpatches outside maintenance windows for critical security CVEs? (cost vs risk tradeoff)
- Automate detection of cache-heavy pods and automatically sequence cache warmups before drain.
- Improve autoscaler integration to pre-warm spare nodes when any drain > 10m expected.

Related artifacts and references:
- ticket: linear/ISSUE-1423 (post-incident notes for node flapping on 2024-07-29)
- github: PR-987 (capacity injector improvements)
- ops note: oncall-cheatsheet-gpu-replacement (see separate doc)

Appendix: postmortem prompts to include in follow-up
- What exactly failed (hardware vs driver vs kernel vs orchestration)?
- Why did automation not remediate? (timeouts, quota, API error)
- Was the communication timeline clear?
- What tests could have caught this earlier?

Status: working draft. Next steps: run a fire-drill with a simulated node-cordon/drain + hotpatch in staging; finalize rollback steps for livepatch; decide policy for emergency livepatch approvals.

Notes to self: leave the diagnostic script output retention to 7 days; rotate diagnostics to cloud storage and attach to incident ticket automatically.
